\chapter{See You Tomorrow}
\label{ch:ar-see-you-tomorrow}
\hlchaptermodality{24}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can part from someone in Arabic with ilā l-ghad, 'until tomorrow'.}

Say ilā l-ghad, point to the ilā already known from ilā l-liqāʾ, and follow gh-d-w from 'dawn' to 'tomorrow'.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ilā l-ghad]{\ar{إلى} \ar{الغد} (ilā l-ghad) — \textquotedblleft{}see you tomorrow,\textquotedblright{} the same ilā again}

\label{lesson:AR-C24-ila-al-ghad}



\begin{quote}
You already have the pattern: \textbf{ilā} + a future point = \textquotedblleft{}see you {[}then{]}.\textquotedblright{} Here it is again, with \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{} filling the slot.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — The two pieces, one already familiar}
\textbf{\ar{إلى} \ar{الغد}} (\emph{ilā l-ghad}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{until tomorrow}\textquotedblright{}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{إلى}} (\emph{ilā}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{until},\textquotedblright{} the exact same word from \emph{ilā l-liqāʾ} (\textquotedblleft{}see you {[}later{]}\textquotedblright{}).
  \item \textbf{\ar{الغد}} (\emph{al-ghad}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{tomorrow},\textquotedblright{} root \textbf{gh-d-w} (\ar{غ}-\ar{د}-\ar{و}).
  \item Note \textbf{\ar{ل}} is a sun letter, so \emph{al-ghad} would assimilate — but \textbf{\ar{غ}} (\emph{ghayn}) is a \textbf{moon letter}, so here the \emph{l} stays put: \emph{al-ghad}, not doubled the way \emph{al-liqāʾ} and \emph{as-salāma} were.
\end{itemize}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{Gh-d-w}'s core sense is \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to go out at dawn, early morning}\textquotedblright{} — and \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{}} grows directly out of that \textquotedblleft{}early morning\textquotedblright{} sense. This is \textbf{not} a one-off coincidence: this \textbf{exact} shift also happened in Latin, where \emph{māne} (\textquotedblleft{}morning\textquotedblright{}) became French's \emph{demain} and Spanish's \emph{mañana} (\textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{}). Two completely unrelated language families — Semitic and Indo-European — independently building \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{} out of \textquotedblleft{}morning.\textquotedblright{}
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ilā l-ghad\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}until tomorrow\textquotedblright{}
  \item the reused piece — ilā, already known from ilā l-liqāʾ
  \item the root echo — gh-d-w, \textquotedblleft{}dawn/morning\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow,\textquotedblright{} the same shift as Latin māne $\to$ mañana/demain
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What word does \textbf{ilā l-ghad} share with \textbf{ilā l-liqāʾ}? (\textbf{Ilā}, \textquotedblleft{}until.\textquotedblright{}) What does the root \textbf{gh-d-w} literally mean, before it comes to mean \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}To go out at dawn, early morning.\textquotedblright{}}) Is this morning-to-tomorrow shift unique to Arabic? (\textbf{No} — Latin's \emph{māne} (\textquotedblleft{}morning\textquotedblright{}) independently became French's \emph{demain} and Spanish's \emph{mañana}, \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow,\textquotedblright{} the same way.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[maʿa s-salāma · ilā l-liqāʾ]{Every way to leave}

\label{lesson:AR-R24-every-way-to-leave}



\begin{quote}
Give both Arabic farewells and the literal meaning of each, without reading on. Then spell the longer one, right to left.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script: the throat sound and the shape-shifter}
\textbf{\ar{ع}} \emph{ʿayn} is two pieces: an \textbf{open-mouth curve} on top, like a small \emph{c} facing left, and a \textbf{bowl} beneath it when the letter stands alone or ends a word. It opens a \textbf{third} dots-family — the bowl and the hook-and-tail were the first two — and its dotted partner is \textbf{\ar{غ}} \emph{ghayn}.

\textbf{\ar{ه}} \emph{hāʾ} is the opposite kind of letter: one closed loop, no dots, and the most \textbf{shape-shifting} thing in the alphabet. It wears four genuinely different coats depending on where it sits in the word.

\subsection*{Script: \ar{مع} \ar{السلامة}, letter by letter}
Write these out:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{مع}} — \emph{mīm}, its round head joining left into \emph{ʿayn}
  \item \textbf{\ar{السلامة}} — \emph{alif · lām}, then \emph{sīn · lām · alif · mīm}, then the tied \textbf{\ar{ة}}
\end{itemize}

Both letters of \textbf{\ar{مع}} were already yours. And \textbf{\ar{السلامة}} is not a long new word: it is \textbf{\ar{الـ}} plus the very first word you ever wrote, plus a tied \emph{tāʾ} on the end.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one pattern, one rule}]
Arabic does not only add endings; it pours a root into a \textbf{shape}. The root \textbf{s–l–m} poured into \emph{faʿāla} turns \emph{peace} into \textbf{the state of safety} — \emph{salām} becomes \emph{salāma}.

Then the sun-letter rule bites: \textbf{\ar{س}} is a sun letter, so the \emph{l} of \textbf{\ar{الـ}} assimilates to it. Written \textbf{\ar{الس}}, said \textbf{as-}salāma.

\textbf{\ar{مع}} \emph{maʿa} is a preposition and it \textbf{stands alone}, unlike \textbf{\ar{الـ}} and \textbf{\ar{بـ}}, which fasten onto the next word.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the other farewell}
\textbf{\ar{إلى} \ar{اللقاء}} \emph{ilā l-liqāʾ} is \textbf{\ar{إلى}} (\emph{until}) plus \textbf{\ar{اللقاء}} (\emph{the meeting}), from the root \textbf{l–q–y}, to meet. So Arabic does not say \emph{goodbye}; it says \textbf{until the meeting} — the same move Spanish makes with \emph{hasta luego}, \emph{until later}.

Two shapes in it run past the writing set: the \textbf{\ar{إ}} with its hamza below, and the \textbf{\ar{ق}} \emph{qāf}. Read them for now.

\subsection*{The exchange}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} greet, give your name, ask after them, and part — the whole arc, to a man
  \item \emph{Say it:} part with safety — \emph{maʿa s-salāma}
  \item \emph{Say it:} part until the meeting — \emph{ilā l-liqāʾ}
  \item \emph{Recall:} the root that both opens the book's greeting and closes its farewell
\end{itemize}

That last one is the joke the language plays on you: \textbf{s–l–m} is the root of the first thing you learned to say and the last. \emph{salām}, \emph{salāma}, \emph{islām}, \emph{muslim} — peace, safety, wholeness, all one family.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the three pieces of \textbf{\ar{السلامة}}. (\textbf{\ar{الـ}} + \emph{salām} + \textbf{\ar{ة}}.) Give the root inside \textbf{\ar{اللقاء}} and its sense. (\textbf{l–q–y}, to meet.) Name the letter that wears four different coats. (\textbf{\ar{ه}}.) And say whether \textbf{\ar{مع}} attaches to the next word. (\textbf{No} — it stands alone.)
\end{tcolorbox}
